title: Built a puzzle game with Codex + Claude. Rotation, snapping and the block generator were the hard parts.
author: leeseifer
selftext:
I used Codex and Claude to build Glowform, a neon tangram-style game for iPhone and iPad. The tricky parts were rotation, snapping and the block generator.

Rotation: two-finger rotation felt awkward, so I moved to 45° buttons and tap-to-rotate. A tap needed to be distinguished from a drag so a small finger movement wouldn't accidentally turn the piece.

Snapping: a piece could line up with an edge but still jump somewhere I didn't intend. The fix was to preserve its position along the edge while closing the gap, then check for overlap when released.

!\[img\](xipt2tza6pqh1)

Block generator: drawing an outline first could leave me with a shape the pieces couldn't fill. Building a valid arrangement first and deriving the outline from it gave each generated puzzle a known solution. Filters then remove holes and duplicate shapes.

The workflow was one bounded task at a time, with an acceptance test defined before coding. That made problems like these easier to isolate.

It's on the App Store if you'd like to try it: \[https://apps.apple.com/app/id6795368135\](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6795368135)

80 puzzles are free with ads; the remaining levels and ad removal are an optional one-time purchase.

For anyone building games with AI: which takes you more iteration, the game logic or getting the controls to feel right?
